key_facts: **Primary localised cutaneous amyloidosis**: amyloid made from **damaged keratinocytes** builds up in the papillary dermis; it is **not** systemic amyloidosis.
Two common forms: **macular** (rippled grey-brown patches, upper back) and **lichen** (very itchy firm papules, shins); they coexist in about a quarter of cases.
Most common in people of **Asian, Middle Eastern and South American** descent with skin types IV–V.
Driven by chronic **friction and scratching** (nylon scrubs, brushes, notalgia paraesthetica); about 10% are familial.
Clinical diagnosis ± biopsy (**Congo red, apple-green birefringence**). Stop friction, potent steroid ± occlusion, treat itch; refer if refractory.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Cutaneous amyloidosis is a group of conditions in which **amyloid** (abnormally folded protein) is deposited in the skin. In the common **primary localised** forms, the amyloid comes from **keratin** released by damaged keratinocytes, and it stays in the skin.

ul: **Macular amyloidosis**: itchy or symptomless, grey-brown, **rippled** (reticulate) pigmentation, usually between the shoulder blades.
**Lichen amyloidosis**: intensely **itchy**, firm, brown, scaly papules on the shins, often in rows, merging into plaques.
**Biphasic** amyloidosis: both forms together.
Rare forms (nodular amyloidosis, which can link to systemic disease) and **systemic** amyloidosis are different conditions needing specialist assessment.

sub: Most common in people from **Asia, the Middle East and South America**, and in **skin types IV–V**.
Usually adults; macular amyloidosis is more common in **women**; lichen amyloidosis is more common in **men** aged 50–60.
Up to **10%** are familial (autosomal dominant, **OSMR** or **IL31RA** genes, part of the itch pathway).
Macular and lichen amyloidosis **coexist in about 25%**.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Chronic **friction and scratching** damage keratinocytes; their keratin is processed into amyloid in the upper dermis.

sub: Nylon towels, bath brushes, loofahs, back scrubbers and rough clothing ("friction amyloidosis").
**Notalgia paraesthetica** (itchy patch below the shoulder blade) often leads to macular amyloidosis.
**Atopic dermatitis** and lichen simplex are linked with lichen amyloidosis.
Familial forms (OSMR, IL31RA); rarely **multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A** (RET mutations) with interscapular amyloidosis.

ul: Sun exposure and darker skin types are risk factors.
Occasionally associated with autoimmune conditions.

fig.caption: Repeated scrubbing of the upper back with a brush or nylon towel is a common trigger of macular amyloidosis.
fig.alt: Person scrubbing the upper back with a long-handled brush

ul: **"It's dirt, so scrub harder"**: scrubbing is the cause and makes it worse.
**"Amyloid in the skin means organ disease"**: localised cutaneous amyloidosis is not systemic amyloidosis.

mech.t: Repeated rubbing or scratching damages basal keratinocytes, which undergo apoptosis.
Keratin filaments from dying cells form **colloid (keratin) bodies** that drop into the papillary dermis, where macrophages and fibroblasts modify them into **amyloid**.
mech.caption: Step 2: damaged basal keratinocytes shed keratin bodies into the papillary dermis.

mech.t: Small globules of amyloid collect in the **dermal papillae** with melanin-laden macrophages, giving the grey-brown colour. In lichen amyloidosis the epidermis thickens over them, forming papules.
mech.caption: Step 3: amyloid globules in the dermal papillae with pigment-laden macrophages; Congo-red staining shows apple-green birefringence (inset).

mech.t: Amyloid and the thickened skin itch, so scratching continues and more amyloid forms. Faults in the **OSMR / IL-31** itch pathway explain familial cases.

histo: Small globules of pink amorphous **amyloid** in the **dermal papillae**, just beneath the epidermis.
Lichen amyloidosis: acanthosis and hyperkeratosis over the deposits.
**Congo red** stains amyloid, with **apple-green birefringence** in polarised light; crystal violet and thioflavin T also help; immunostaining shows keratin origin.
Deposits can be sparse, so multiple sections or a deeper biopsy may be needed.

ul: **Itch**: mild or absent in macular amyloidosis, often **severe and persistent** in lichen amyloidosis.
Cosmetic concern about pigmentation.

lesions.name: Rippled grey-brown macules
lesions.t: Small dusky macules merge into a **rippled or reticulate** pattern.

lesions.name: Interscapular patch
lesions.t: Ill-defined pigmentation between the shoulder blades.

lesions.name: Firm itchy papules
lesions.t: Tan-brown, scaly, dome-shaped papules, often in rows, on the shins.

lesions.name: Confluent plaques
lesions.t: Papules merge into thickened, ridged plaques.

bodymap.caption: Macular amyloidosis on the upper back, shoulders and upper arms; lichen amyloidosis on the shins.
pts: **Macular**: interscapular back, upper chest, shoulders and outer upper arms.
**Lichen**: shins, then thighs, forearms and the backs of the hands.

variants.name: Macular amyloidosis
variants.t: Rippled grey-brown patches, upper back; women; friction.

variants.name: Notalgia-linked macular amyloidosis
variants.t: Pigmented patch below one shoulder blade from chronic scratching of notalgia paraesthetica.

variants.name: Lichen amyloidosis
variants.t: Intensely itchy papules on the shins; atopy.

variants.name: Biphasic
variants.t: Both forms together in about a quarter.

variants.name: Nodular amyloidosis
variants.t: Waxy nodules; light-chain amyloid; may relate to plasma cell disorders: specialist work-up.

sub: The most affected group; pigmentation is often the main concern and can be confused with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Ask about relatives; consider MEN2A in familial interscapular amyloidosis (specialist).

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Diagnosis is usually **clinical** from the rippled pattern, site and history of friction or itch.

ul: Scrubbing habits, brushes, towels; chronic itch; atopy; family history.
Systemic symptoms (to exclude systemic amyloidosis): tiredness, weight loss, purpura, enlarged tongue, swelling, frothy urine.
**Dermoscopy**: a central white or brown hub with surrounding pigment.
**Skin biopsy** with Congo red when the diagnosis is uncertain.
If systemic or nodular amyloidosis is suspected: specialist investigations (serum and urine protein electrophoresis, free light chains).

ddx.name: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
ddx.f: Follows a known rash; no ripple; no papules.

ddx.name: Lichen planus pigmentosus
ddx.f: Grey-brown patches on the face, neck and flexures; may follow lichen planus.

ddx.name: Hypertrophic lichen planus
ddx.f: Thick violaceous plaques on the shins; Wickham striae; biopsy.

ddx.name: Lichen simplex chronicus / prurigo
ddx.f: Single lichenified plaque or nodules from scratching; no amyloid on biopsy.

ddx.name: Acanthosis nigricans
ddx.f: Velvety pigmentation in the flexures and neck; insulin resistance.

ddx.name: Pretibial myxoedema
ddx.f: Waxy plaques on shins with thyroid eye disease.

ul: Break the **itch–scratch–friction** cycle; set realistic expectations: pigment improves slowly and recurs if friction restarts.
Treatment is often difficult; many options are specialist and evidence is limited.
**Stop scrubbing**: no loofahs, brushes or nylon towels; soft, loose clothing.
Regular **emollients**; keep nails short.
Sun protection for pigmentation.

drugs.name: Potent topical corticosteroid
drugs.use: Itch and lichen amyloidosis; occlusion improves effect.
drugs.cautions: Limit courses and monitor for atrophy, especially under occlusion.

drugs.name: Topical calcineurin inhibitor
drugs.use: Itch where long-term steroid is unwanted.

drugs.name: Sedating antihistamine at night
drugs.use: To help sleep when itch is severe; does not treat the itch mechanism.

drugs.name: Specialist options
drugs.use: Intralesional steroid, topical capsaicin or DMSO, phototherapy (NB-UVB, PUVA), oral acitretin, laser or dermabrasion for lichen amyloidosis.

ladder.t: Potent topical steroid ± occlusion, or calcineurin inhibitor; night sedating antihistamine if sleep is affected.

refer.t: Severe or refractory itch, diagnostic doubt (biopsy), or for specialist treatments.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

refer.t: Purpura (especially around the eyes), enlarged tongue, nerve symptoms, heart or kidney symptoms: possible **systemic** amyloidosis.
Waxy nodules (nodular amyloidosis): screen for plasma cell disease.

ul: Persistent itch, sleep disturbance and lichenification.
Long-lasting **cosmetic** pigmentation and distress.
Steroid side effects with long courses under occlusion.
**Chronic** and benign; it does not progress to systemic amyloidosis.
Improves slowly once friction and scratching stop; tends to recur.

pearls: Ask about **back scrubbers, brushes and nylon towels**: stopping them is the key treatment.
Rippled interscapular pigmentation in skin of colour is often macular amyloidosis, not dirt or PIH.
An itchy patch under one shoulder blade suggests **notalgia paraesthetica**.
Potent steroid under occlusion helps lichen amyloidosis, but time-limit courses.
Localised cutaneous amyloid is **not** systemic amyloidosis; refer if systemic features appear.
Related: [phytophotodermatitis](condition:phytophotodermatitis) (the other half of the Module 6 · Week 3 topic).

quiz.q: Where does the amyloid in macular and lichen amyloidosis come from?

quiz.a: Congo red, with apple-green birefringence under polarised light.
Stop scrubbing with brushes, loofahs or nylon towels.

quiz.q: Does it progress to systemic amyloidosis?
quiz.a: No; systemic features need separate specialist assessment.
